keyPoints.line: a cold box right under the tap.

read.where: The Draught Beer Quality Manual names the designs. **Direct draw**: kegs in a refrigerated cabinet or walk-in right behind the faucets, the short trip kept cold by the box itself. **Air-cooled long draw**: a fan pushes cold air from the cooler through a duct around the lines, good for about **15 ft** with a **single** duct and **25 ft** with a **double** duct; it’s sensitive to hot rooms. **Glycol-cooled long draw**: for runs **longer than 25 ft**, a chiller pumps food-grade glycol along the beer lines, set to **29–32°F**. Glycol needs care: check the bath temperature **every two weeks**, motors, pumps and condenser **monthly**.
read.mixup: Glycol cools the lines, not the kegs. The kegs still live in a walk-in at **34–38°F**.

video.title: Minute with a Master Cicerone - Primary and Secondary Regulators

read.bigIdea: The gas ends up in the beer.
read.where: As a keg drains, the gas fills it, so impurities **go into the beer**. Use **beverage-grade** gas: the International Society of Beverage Technologists sets CO2 purity at **99.9%** minimum; nitrogen generators should make at least **99.7%**. A **gas filter** helps; change it on the maker’s schedule. **Never** use compressed air: its oxygen brings **stale, cardboard** flavors within hours. Leaks waste gas and drop pressure, which causes **foamy** beer; listen and feel for them at the connections. The manual’s general settings: direct draw on 100% CO2 **12–15 psi**; long draw on a rich blend (60–80% CO2) **22–25 psi**; nitro beer on 25/75 at **30–35 psi**.
read.mixup: Turning the gas up doesn’t fix a slow pour. It over-carbonates the beer; the balance is set once and held.

read.bigIdea: Every two weeks, every quarter, every six months.
read.where: Level 3 taught how to clean; running the program means owning the **calendar**. The Draught Beer Quality Manual: every **two weeks**, a caustic line clean, every faucet **taken apart**, couplers **scrubbed**, FOBs cleaned in line. **Quarterly**, an **acid** clean to remove beer stone. **Every six months**, FOBs and couplers fully **disassembled**. Replace **vinyl jumper and direct-draw lines every one to two years**, or any time there’s an infection; replace long-draw **trunk line** at **10 years** or when flavors carry between lines. If a service cleans for us, we still check their work: the **log** should show a clean within the last two weeks.
read.mixup: An acid clean is **in addition** to the caustic clean, never instead of it.

keyPoints.line: in the walk-in, air and liquid.

read.bigIdea: Check the system the way a guest tastes it.
read.where: Once a month, walk the system with a checklist built from the Draught Beer Quality Manual. **Cooler**: air and a liquid thermometer at **36–38°F**; lines full, no kinks; gauges at their settings; no hiss. **Bar**: beer served at **38–44°F**, pouring about **2 oz a second**. **Hygiene**: the cleaning log shows the last clean within **two weeks**; scrape inside a faucet with a **straw** and smell the coupler and spill tray: **vinegar or butter** means bacteria; FOB sight glasses clear, jumper lines clear and **unstained**. Write it down and fix what fails.
read.mixup: A clean-looking faucet can still be dirty inside. The straw test and the smell tell you; the outside doesn’t.

sources: Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual, 4th ed., 2019 (brewersassociation.org); House practice (ours; GM to confirm). Written for Mise in our own words, Nov 14, 2026.

unverified: The Draught Beer Quality Manual gives vinyl jumper lines two figures: “every one to two years” in its line-replacement guidelines and “every two years” in its inspection checklist. The page says one to two years.
Our own system (direct draw, air or glycol), gas supplier and pressure settings: GM to confirm with our draft service. Pressures on the page are the manual’s general ranges, not our settings.
Running the audit monthly is house practice; the manual’s checks are daily (pre-shift) and every cleaning.
